subtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE STUDY OF FUNDS FOR MEDICAL RESEARCH-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
PROPOSED COMMITTEE STUDY OF FUNDS FOR MEDICAL RESEARCH-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Considering that it is always easier to prevent than to cure and that preventive medicine should be the goal of the Minister of National Health and Welfare, considering also that medical research is the main and most important element of any preventive program because research makes it possible to face future problems, and considering finally that control measures in the field of medical research jeopardize the future health of Canadians, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That this House or its Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs consider forthwith the matter of the medical research budget so that the available funds be sufficient to provide for the fastest progress in the field of preventive medicine and thus meet the main priority, namely the present and future health of Canadians.

OIL-REASON FOR REJECTING BLENDED PRICING CONCEPT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was going to say "in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources", but I see him coming in just now. Can the minister tell us why the federal government has
rejected the blended pricing concept for oil, given the fact that it is alleged this process would provide incentives for oil exploration and production and at the same time provide additional protection for consumers?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REJECTING BLENDED PRICING CONCEPT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is the very problem. There is no evidence that the proposal will indeed provide the kind of incentives to which the hon. member refers. The other problem is that the Ontario government has not demonstrated how, if you freeze the price of old oil at $8, with declining production you will generate more cash funds which are needed for exploration and development.

subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REJECTING BLENDED PRICING CONCEPT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: Would the minister not agree, though, that by taking the position he is now taking he is prejudging one of the items which will be put forward at the conference, presumably starting within the next day or two, and is it appropriate for the government to reject a position which is going to be presented there even before there is an opportunity for the people supporting that proposition to put it forward?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REJECTING BLENDED PRICING CONCEPT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: I am very much looking forward to an articulation by the province of Ontario as to how this would work, but up until now the province of Ontario has not demonstrated how it would meet either one of the two points I have made: one is the incentive question, and the other is the provision of cash flow.

subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REJECTING BLENDED PRICING CONCEPT-GOVERNMENT POSITION

subtopic: OIL-REASON FOR REJECTING BLENDED PRICING CONCEPT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext: The discussion will take place. There will be other different points of view put forward. I am sure the federal government will have its view. There are many different provinces involved. As far as I know there is only one province which has even flirted with the idea the government of Ontario put forward. None of the others has supported it.

subtopic: FINANCE
FINANCE
subsubtopic: REASON FOR DECLINE IN BALANCE OF TRADE IN MANUFACTURED GOODS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my questions are for the Minister of Finance, and they relate to some of the information placed before the House last Friday in the "Economic Review". The conclusions of the review are not clear, and because the information in the review will form the basis of the coming debate, it is important for us to know what conclusions the minister has drawn from the statistics which were presented.
In looking at the productivity figures in the manufacturing sector, the review points out that for the last three years increases in labour costs per unit of output have been lower in Canada than in the United States, and the graph dramatically points that out. How, then, does the minister account for our sharp decline in the balance of trade in manufactured goods? Surely the minister cannot hold increases in labour rates in Canada responsible for that.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: REASON FOR DECLINE IN BALANCE OF TRADE IN MANUFACTURED GOODS WITH UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some of the conclusions to be drawn from the "Economic Review" will be dealt with at some length in the budget. The drop in Canadian exports over the past year-not just in the last several quarters-has been due to

a rather less buoyant condition in the United States market in particular, but in other export markets as well, than was the case in the Canadian market. Certainly, in the early years of the period covered, the disincentive was not the Canadian labour cost. However, the concern of the government of Canada was that with the rate of wage settlements which were contemplated in September and October 1975, namely the 30 per cent, 40 per cent and 50 per cent settlements being sought at that time, then any trend of that kind would be directly adverse to the rate of productivity in Canada.

subtopic: INFLATIONARY EFFECT OF INCREASED PROFITS- GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CONTROL
INFLATIONARY EFFECT OF INCREASED PROFITS- GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CONTROL
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. On a number of occasions the minister has stated that wage and salary increases- and he is restating it today-are going to make our international trading position uncompetitive. In the "Economic Review" labour costs per unit of output have increased by 38.9 per cent since 1972; however, despite a decline in 1975, profits per unit of output have increased by some 62.9 per cent. Is the minister prepared to express his concern about this kind of inflation in demand, and can he indicate what he intends to do about the increase in profits as compared to the increase in wage and salaries?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subtopic: INFLATIONARY EFFECT OF INCREASED PROFITS- GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CONTROL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is because we are concerned about both wage and salary increases-which I would remind the hon. gentleman make up two-thirds of the gross national product- and increases in profits that we put forward the anti-inflation program which touches equally on controls of profits and of incomes.

DECLINE IN PRODUCTIVITY-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CORRECT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. As productivity figures released last Friday by the Department of Finance show that during the past two years there has been a sharp and accelerating decrease in productivity which has been the major factor in increasing unemployment and inflation, when will the Prime Minister take the House into his confidence and tell the House, as he promised three months ago, on February 5, how the government intends to correct this serious situation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DECLINE IN PRODUCTIVITY-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO CORRECT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to give my office notice of his intended question. I have asked to be informed of the status of the various works in progress on which I reported to the hon. member about a couple of months ago. The work is progressing well. I am advised that it is important not to draw extreme conclusions from the cyclical slowdown in productivity which took place in 1973 and 1975. The dominant factor was the economic recession. The counterpart to this slowdown is expected to be above-trend productivity increases in the next year or two.

They also arrange with Canada Manpower Centres on a daily basis to have workers brought in from outside the local area, as they are required, (b) Regionally, particularly in Ontario and Quebec, radio stations will be used for frequent spot announcements to outline current situations in the fruit, vegetable and tobacco harvests, (c) Nationally, brochures and fact sheets are used to inform potential employers and workers of the services available at the Canada Farm Labour Pools and Canada Manpower Centres (CMCs). During peak demand periods, the CMCs of agricultural manpower supply and demand areas are in daily contact with each other to make sure that workers are at the disposal of employers when required.
2. The Department already sponsors a program designed to attract young Canadians, primarily students, to agricultural work during the summer vacation period and to possible future careers in agriculture. Known as Agriculture for Young Canadians, the program features federal participation in the establishment of new or existing agricultural manpower programs for youth, operated by the provinces and cost-shared under the provisions of the existing Federal-Provincial Agricultural Manpower Agreements. The program was initiated in 1974 and, to date, the Provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia have participated. Inexperienced students, as well as other workers, who obtain seasonal agricultural employment through any of the Department's agencies are eligible to receive up to four days training with full wages. This assistance is provided at no cost to the agricultural employers under the Canada Farm Labour Pool's worker orientation program. Graduate students who wish to enter farming or food processing as an occupation have always been eligible to receive training directly from employers participating in the Canada Manpower Industrial Training Program."]

speechtext:
1.	Has the government ended the STOL demonstration four months early and, if so, for what reason?
2.	How much was budgeted for the STOL demonstration and how much of the budget was and will be spent?
3.	What were the projected and actual (a) capital, (b) operating costs of the demonstration?
4.	How much revenue was collected from STOL passengers and did it cover the operating costs?
5.	Will DOT and Airtransit employees who worked on the STOL demonstration be re-assigned or released?
6.	(a) What will be the disposition of the equipment used in the STOL demonstration, (b) will it be used in other (i) sections of DOT, (ii) departments and, if so, is this future use reflected in the 1976-77 Estimates?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: STOL DEMONSTRATION PROJECT
speechtext:
1. The STOL demonstration is to end four months early on April 30, 1976 because the objectives of the project will have been met by that date, and the monies budgeted to the program will have been expended by that date.
2.	A total of $24,411 million was budgeted for the STOL demonstration project. On April 30, 1976, it is estimated that this budget will have been overrun by $124,000.
3.	The projected capital and operating costs of the demonstration were $15.5 million and $8.9 million, respectively. The actual capital and operating costs to April 30, 1976 are estimated at $15.5 million and $9,035 million respectively.
4.	Total revenues collected from STOL passengers up to the end of February amounted to $3,378 million. It is
May 3, 1976

estimated that by April 30, 1976, total revenues collected from passengers will have amounted to approximately $3.6 million. These revenues do not cover the operating costs.
5.	Term employees with Transport Canada, will be reassigned where positions are available. Otherwise, they will be released. Indeterminate Transport Canada employees will be re-assigned. Air Canada has been working very closely with Airtransit to ensure that all employees of Airtransit are given full consideration for any Air Canada job vacancies for which they are qualified. A number have already been hired by Air Canada. Also, Air Canada employees who were seconded to Airtransit are being reabsorbed on an individual basis consistent with commitments made to them when they were seconded.

MANPOWER-AVAILABILITY OF SEASONAL JOBS IN AGRICULTURE, 1976
speechtext:
1. Is the Department of Manpower and Immigration taking any action
to advertise nationally the availability of seasonal jobs to assist farmers and food processors in the growing, harvesting and processing of the 1976 fruit, tobacco and vegetable crops and, if so, what is such action?
2. Has any consideration been given to tying-in the farm labour shortage each year with a training programme for students who may want to enter farming and food processing as an occupation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: MANPOWER-AVAILABILITY OF SEASONAL JOBS IN AGRICULTURE, 1976
speechtext:
1. A national advertising campaign will not be undertaken by the Department to make known the availability of seasonal jobs in agriculture in 1976. However, a national advertising campaign is already underway advising students to register with their local Canada Manpower Centre for Students. Students who register there or with other Canada Manpower offices are informed of any available seasonal agricultural employment. In addition, the Department will offer service to both farmers and workers through the network of Canada Farm Labour Pools (CFLP) during the coming months. During the peak manpower demand periods there will be no less than 78

May 3, 1976

points of service, some 62 of which are operated year round. Publicity and advertising is again being organized at all levels to ensure that the employment needs of both the farmers and the agricultural workers will be met. (a) Locally, CFLPs advertise the need for workers in local newspapers. They also arrange with Canada Manpower Centres on a daily basis to have workers brought in from outside the local area, as they are required, (b) Regionally, particularly in Ontario and Quebec, radio stations will be used for frequent spot announcements to outline current situations in the fruit, vegetable and tobacco harvests, (c) Nationally, brochures and fact sheets are used to inform potential employers and workers of the services available at the Canada Farm Labour Pools and Canada Manpower Centres (CMCs). During peak demand periods, the CMCs of agricultural manpower supply and demand areas are in daily contact with each other to make sure that workers are at the disposal of employers when required.
2. The Department already sponsors a program designed to attract young Canadians, primarily students, to agricultural work during the summer vacation period and to possible future careers in agriculture. Known as Agriculture for Young Canadians, the program features federal participation in the establishment of new or existing agricultural manpower programs for youth, operated by the provinces and cost-shared under the provisions of the existing Federal-Provincial Agricultural Manpower Agreements. The program was initiated in 1974 and, to date, the Provinces of Ontario, Manitoba, Alberta and British Columbia have participated. Inexperienced students, as well as other workers, who obtain seasonal agricultural employment through any of the Department's agencies are eligible to receive up to four days training with full wages. This assistance is provided at no cost to the agricultural employers under the Canada Farm Labour Pool's worker orientation program. Graduate students who wish to enter farming or food processing as an occupation have always been eligible to receive training directly from employers participating in the Canada Manpower Industrial Training Program.

On December 18, 1975, I announced expenditure reductions of the order of $1.5 billion during the 1976-77 fiscal year. Of course, these reductions were part of the government program to curb inflation. Among them were measured to end some programs, to cancel indexing of family allowances, to reduce costs approved for some Crown corporations and to freeze certain payments to members of

May 3, 1976
Members' Salaries
the House of Commons and the Senate, officials and Crown corporations agents whose salaries are in the upper brackets.
At that time I mentioned that certain pieces of legislations had to be amended to make those cutbacks; I was the one who the day after tabled this bill whose purpose is to delay until the beginning of 1977 the escalation of the sessional allowances of members of the Senate and the House of Commons, which would have automatically taken place at the end of the year 1975; to delay until 1977 the escalation of the extra salaries and allowances payable to ministers, parliamentary secretaries and other members of the Senate and House of Commons receiving remuneration over and above their sessional allowance; for the year 1976, limit to $200 the portion of the monthly increase in the supplementary retirement benefit that is attributable to the 11.3 per cent rise in the Benefit Index during the 12 months ending September 30, 1975.
On December 18, 1975, I announced that we could save $600,000 in this way; according to our latest estimates, we will be able to save nearly $750,000. As the House leader said on Thursday, April 29 last, I will be moving in due time an amendment to this bill to freeze also expense allowances as well as current salaries for 1976. It is anticipated that Bill C-87, the Government Expenditures Restraint Act, will be given second reading soon.
As to the level of pay of the senior staff in the public service and crown corporations, I repeat that it will be frozen, that is maintained at the current level by an administrative measure, until April 1, 1977.
Mr. Speaker, if members of the Senate and the House of Commons examined this Bill C-81 diligently the Canadian people would know that we are capable of making very great sacrifices.
I hope that people, particularly those who are sometimes very cynical about members of this House, will understand that they are making an enormous personal sacrifice today. I think the salaries that members currently receive are really too low for good members, and I will defend that before any audience. There are thousands of people in the public service and crown corporations who are paid much more than private members. But, once again, for the good of the community, members decided to make enormous sacrifices by waving any increase in their salaries or with respect to their expenses for the current year. What I regret, Mr. Speaker-
This measure was announced last December, and there were very few people in the land who gave any credit to members of parliament for that. We imposed that kind of sacrifice upon ourselves. I am not talking about myself. I am a minister and I can survive with my salary, but I know many members of parliament who do not make much money, who have to go into their riding, who are not assisted by all sorts of organizations, yet they are ready to impose that sacrifice upon themselves. When we got a little increase a few months ago, there were all sorts of articles all over Canada blaming members of parliament. I consider $24,000 a very small salary for a person who represents thousands of people in the House of Commons every week

from Monday to Friday night, who flies or drives back to his riding every weekend, who works 12 hours a day, and so on.

I recognized that the minister said "pay"; he did not say "income". But I could smell what was taking place. As soon as he sat down, I was recognized and I put the following question to the President of the Treasury Board, as reported at page 10165 of Hansard:

Mr. Speaker, that applies to the members' salaries.

The bill does not stop with the clauses which amend the Senate and House of Commons Act. It also contains clauses amending the Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act. The aim of that amendment is to make sure that no one, in 1976, will get an escalation in his pension beyond a certain amount, and this applies not just to members of parliament but to retired public servants, retired members of the armed forces, retired members of the RCMP, and so on. It applies to anyone getting any kind of pension coming under the government. The provision is that no one is to get an increase amounting to more than $2,400 a year. This, I submit, is a good idea. I would remind hon. members that there are lots of Canadians who never see a pension from their work amounting to $200 a month. We are simply saying that no one should get an increase, in 1976, of an amount greater than $200 a month. We certainly support that limitation.
I regret that when the President of the Treasury Board brought in a bill containing this clause he did not see fit to deal with some other things as well. He proposed a measure to prevent certain persons from getting pensions which would be too high, but I regret he did not bring in a provision to correct a situation which we thought would be corrected last December when we were dealing with Bill C-52. I refer to the fact that retired members of the armed Forces, the RCMP and others are obliged to wait until they are 60 before their pensions are escalated unless they can qualify under a rule which is sometimes known as the 85 rule.
When we were dealing with Bill C-52 last December, it looked for a time as though that rule would be modified, and I had hoped we might have dealt with this matter by way of the legislation presently before us. In other words, while we are seeking to ensure that some persons should not receive pensions which are too high, we should also seek to deal with the positions of those who are not getting the escalation they should be entitled to receive. I hope we can deal with this aspect in the committee or at the report stage.
After this quiet speech, despite the cut-calls and interruptions, I am happy to say we shall support, Bill C-81.

If I objected, it was mainly in order that the people, at least those who receive Hansard, be better informed on the subject of members' salaries and allowances.
Had the first motion gone through, everything would have gone under the veil of silence as usual, and the people would have gone on reading all kinds of suggestions concerning our salaries. I want to point out I have no grudge against newspapermen. Only, I resent that some of them take pleasure, when referring to member's salaries, in including both indemnity and allowances under salaries paid. Imagine the reaction by people believing that our salary is tax free. This is unfair to the greater majority of
Members' Salaries
newspapermen. I commend those stating the the salary is $24,000, the allowances are such and such a figure, but the salary is subject to income tax, and therefore if a member gets $24,000 and pays $4,500 in income tax, his net salary is only $18,500. The press have a duty to tell that story to the people, if they are to really inform the poeple.
Of course, allowances are tax free. Nowhere in industry or the public service are officials' expense allowances taxable. The contrary would be impossible and irrational. Why should our expense allowances be taxable? They must be deductible, as those of senior officials, considering the higher cost of living.
I refer directly to the President of the Privy Council. I did not think him capable of dealing that way. Usually he practices consultation, he acts in a less unilateral way. But today, he introduced an amazing piece of legislation. If the MP's expenses are frozen, finally they will be the ones who absorb the higher prices granted big companies, oil and other. I changed car this year, and it cost me $800 more than last year. I use it in my riding to work for my constituents. Some may find this odd but, in my riding, people find it strange because they have never seen, in 14 years, a federal member of Parliament go around visiting the riding. But for 14 years now-the federal Parliament really does exist-people see the federal MP go about the riding. May I say to the hon. members and the people that to go around our riding costs something, especially in the rural ridings.
And I say that the motion moved by the minister today, the amendment to Bill C-81, discriminates against rural members of parliament. I would like to quote some figures. We are not all in the same situation as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who stays in Ottawa and never goes anywhere else. Mr. Speaker, I live 500 miles from here; each week, I must drive 1,000 miles before covering from 300 to 500 miles in to my constituency on Saturdays and Sundays.
I drive an average of 40,000 miles a year for the government. If people want to see my figures, I will show them. Last year, with what the government paid me, I had a deficit of $2,842. This does not matter since I depend on my two companies to make ends meet. But I agree with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) when he says that if a member of parliament must subsist on his allowance alone, be will starve, and I have said so for 14 years. A member who has only his allowance must either starve or do nothing in his constituency, and if he does nothing, he will not last long in his constituency these days. This is why members of parliament who have only a salary and expense allowances live very frugally. They do not need to say so, they live very frugally. This is why I speak on their behalf today. I speak on behalf of all members who represent rural constituencies. When you have to drive 100 or 125 miles to meet a group of senior citizens who are unable to travel, this costs money, and we do not receive one penny for these trips, while members of legislative assemblies receive 10 cents a mile for their travels. I can assure hon. members that at the federal level, we look like beggars.

When the President of the Treasury Board introduced the bill to reduce salaries on December 18, 1975, I was in favour of a salary freeze. I was in favour of such a move even though it was completely different from the theories that are accepted for other workers. See how stupid we are in this House, if I may use this expression. We allow, and I speak of all other workers, increases of at least 12 per cent to be accepted, and increases of 12 per cent, 10 per cent or 8 per cent, and what do we do to give the example? We do not even allow ourselves a 7 per cent rise in the cost of living. Would you believe! In the constituencies, we pass for idiots. Of course, Mr. Speaker, it is certainly to meet the wishes of the government, because some ministers are afraid of losing their job; as for me, I am not afraid, when they vote against me, I shall go back home singing, and as long as I am elected, people will have to put up with me and I intend to go on saying the truth in my constituency. When I meet intelligent people in the departments, I say so, and when I meet idiots, I say so as well.
Mr. Speaker, I know that today most members do not support this particular motion. It is not because they like money, but because they are tired of trying to boost the government's popularity, the popularity of politics. I think that a member's salary should be at least that of a high official who earns $30,000 a year; 16t the journalists note this figure, high government officials make $28,000, $29,000, $30,000, $32,000, $40,000, $42,000 a year, excluding their expenses. And I repeat, this year, their expenses will not be reduced and, mind you, I do not blame them, I admire them, because they know how to look after themselves, they are clever, their expenses will not be reduced by a single cent. They will pay and if the price of gas goes up to $1, they will pay $1. But us, if the price of gas goes up to $1, we will have to make a gift to the government and say: For our good government, let us pay out of our own pockets. Imagine that!
Once again, if they want changes, if they want to standardize things-I have been asking this for a long time-all they need to do is to give us the status of high government officials. Yes, the status of high government officials and let us be paid $32,000 a year plus an expense account. Wait and see at the end of the year when I submit my expense account, there will be much to be paid. Instead of $10,000, the expenditures will be around $25,000. Let us be allowed expense accounts. But no, we are restricted and we have to pay the difference. Then, we have to provide service that is in adequate, unsatisfactory in our riding.
I feel that the government is now working not only against members of parliament but also against the rural people. Today the government wants to prevent those people from receiving the services they are entitled to get from their members in their constituencies. Again, the salary does not matter to me. But as regards expenses, I shall not give up. If the government wants to freeze expenses, it should first freeze the prices asked by big companies. We have been asking that for a long time. The government keeps knocking down wages, but it should first freeze the prices of all those big companies, for they are at the root of inflation. Why not touch them? The government will come begging members of parliament again in order to save these big corporations.

Mr. Speaker, I am fed up, tired of all this sham and I simply ask the President of the Treasury Board, if he is honest and sincere, to withdraw his amendment.
I was listening a moment ago to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and I wonder which of the two has the power. He or the President of the Privy Council? Mr. Speaker, I think this debate is totally superfluous. This bill should not be before us. I do not suppose any woman giving birth to quintuplets would go through what we went through in setting the salaries of members of parliament with a formula to take care of cost of living increases. We had a fight among members of this House on all sides, and with the press and media: that is where the opposition was.
That having been settled, now we have what I suggest is a totally hypocritical and cosmetic action by the government, through the lips of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The blame lies right there. It is said that members of parliament should forgo the cost of living increase in their salaries. Nothing is said about expenses. Of course nothing is said about expenses, and quite rightly so. The world was not discovered yesterday. We have seen the tribulations of members of parliament on all sides. We have seen good members of parliament driven out of this House because of the financial exigencies of their position.
I agree with the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). Those who speak against increasing salaries of members of parliament who must meet the obligations of their position either have an independent income or sit here in a corner in Ottawa and do not know what the constituency problems are. They do not know what it is to maintain a separate home in a constituency and one in Ottawa, or to maintain an apartment here. They do not know what it is to drive an automobile in a constituency, whether urban or rural. I have an urban constituency. I marvel at my colleagues in this House who represent rural constituencies when I see how they are able to absorb, without loud protest, the cost of moving around in that constituency at today's prices. What about the cost of hotels, the price of meals, the price of gasoline and the cost of automobile repairs? It is only a self-deluded fool who would say that these costs have not gone up. A member of parliament is supposed to absorb those costs out of his salary.
The union official, the teacher, the newspaper reporter, the news editor or anyone else who goes on official travel can deduct the cost as a business expense. They are compensated for the increase in those expenditures. However, the elected official, be he a school board trustee, a municipal councillor, a city alderman, a member of a provincial legislature, or a member of this House, is dismissed. He cannot absorb that cost. What public hypocrisy that represents! That is what I object to. I have been in this House for nearly 20 years and I object to these double standards.
The businessman is entitled to deduct his expenses in the course of business at the level of the expenditures. The union officials, the CLC officials who came to Ottawa the other day, will be able to collect their expenses and be reimbursed on the basis of today's costs. They are able to do it at any time. We have the situation in respect of the

teachers and all the officials moving around. Do not think that all the shifting around of the officials we have in respect of labour unrest at the present time does not represent a great expense. Those men and women do not give up one penny from their pockets for that. All along the line in the public service, pensions are escalated to meet cost of living increases. Old age pensions are escalated in order to meet cost of living increases. Veterans pensions are escalated to meet cost of living increases.

They were denied in respect of family allowances; that is right. But all along the line pensions have been escalated. After that nauseous, hypocritical debate of last year with regard to the salaries of members of parliament, when a negotiated conclusion was reached about the first thing that was done by the government in order to, shall we say, sweeten the pill with regard to denying the vast salary increases to senior public servants who just previously had had a salary increase was to deny this to members of parliament.
This is purely a cosmetic and unwarranted gesture. The elected officials in this country are a small number of people dispersed in every constituency. In a school board district there may be six, eight or ten representatives. In a rural municipality or country there may be a few dozen representatives. In a city there may be from 6 to 20 aider-men. The members of a provincial legislature may total 105 or 110 across the country. We are 264. We are easy game to pick off. How do we react? People come down to this place to observe, and with less than two of three month's experience in how this complicated shop operates they are prepared to levy judgment on individual members and tell this place how it should be run. They do not even know their way to the head, to use a nautical term. If they had been here a couple of years, maybe they would have discovered the way to the head and then they would have decided how to run the bridge. I know I will not make any friends with this speech, and I do not intend to. However, I will say this; if I and the hon. member for Roberval and a few others intend to make ourselves the self-appointed ombudsmen on behalf of elected officials, I am quite prepared to do it because I think there is something fundamental to be said all through our system of government on behalf of the elected people.
I will not go into the various motives of why elected representatives seek office. But having sought office and having been rewarded with the confidence of the people, many hon. members-and I look to the left at my colleagues, all the way down to the NDP and the Creditistes, as well as to the government side-men and women who would have had far greater success in other occupations have given them up. Something that all too often John Public in the street, the reporters, their editors, and, God bless them, their publishers, seem to forget is that until you get into this game there is no way of knowing how your own personal occupation will be affected.
Those full-time parliamentarians who are professional men have seen their practices wiped out because this is a

Mr. Speaker, I listened with some enjoyment to the last two speeches. They were reminiscent of all the speeches which have been made on the occasions when pay for members of parliament was discussed. I thought we had got away from that. We got to the stage of setting up a commission at considerable expense. In fact, we did that twice, and a number of suggestions they put forward finally were enacted in legislation, including such things as an escalation clause attached to the composite wage index. This seems to be a fair and reasonable way of handling the situation. It is much more fair than members having to make decisions periodically. There are some of us who believe that our expenses are detached from our salaries, that they are separate and there is merit in some of those separations.
Mr. Speaker, I very much resent the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went on television and used our salaries and expenses as the basis for eliminating some desirable and some less than desirable programs-LIP, LEAP, CYC, and one that I consider to be very advantageous, the indexing of family allowances. He indicated that he was going to cut down on the civil service. In my opinion that has not been done, and in fact a very poor example has been set in the Prime Minister's own office where a number of people have been added to his staff. The Prime Minister suggested on that telecast that members of parliament were going to help him justify his austerity program and set an example for the country.
I intend to move an amendment to the amendment that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) has indicated he will introduce. I think this is the worst kind of legislation we could possibly have, where the government puts up a kite to test whether they can satisfy the public or even members of parliament. They went halfway; they put the freeze on salaries but they did not put it on the pay which included expenses. Now, after nearly six months, they have decided to amend the bill and ask for a recall of the pay that has already been collected on the expenses.

This is the worst of two worlds, Mr. Speaker, and what the government has done is a disgrace. They have delayed making a decision and putting a bill before this House for almost six months to freeze the salary increase that would have been obtained by the index. They have listened to the public and decided they have to add the expenses to the freeze as well. If they had found the public was not interested, this bill would never have been called but would have been allowed to die on the order paper.
I am sympathetic to some of the remarks that have been made. We have set a standard that can be justified. The index takes into consideration most of the negotiated contracts in other civil service fields. That criteria has been applied to our salary and the cost of living has been used in the expenses. That seems reasonable to me, but it also seems an idle gesture to make the compromise we are making in this bill and to add the amendment that the President of the Treasury Board intends to introduce.
Today we have been informed that Canada will spend a billion dollars to buy a number of outdated aircraft which are not suitable for the job they are intended for. No one in a responsible position has indicated that they can justify the role played by the Argus aircraft which they are to replace. I think the government's position is similar to that of Mayor Drapeau: when that billion dollars is multiplied over the years, it will probably amount to about $3 billion. The amount of money involved annually for the expense allowances of members of parliament is approximately $185,000. I think the government should not be allowed to pass this kind of restrictive legislation after they have tested the wind.

subsubtopic: MEASURK RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
that Bill C-84, to amend the Criminal Code in relation to the punishment for murder and certain other serious offences, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on opening the debate on Bill C-84 I am sure all of us are aware that we are beginning the latest instalment of a very old debate. Hon. members who have been here for ten years, as I have, will be participating in their fourth full-scale debate on capital punishment.
I am hoping that the House leaders will be able to work out a formal agreement among all parties that speakers will be limited to 20 minutes. I had prepared a much longer and more detailed speech, going into each of my arguments in some depth. However, in order to stay within 20 minutes I have cut the length of my speech so that we may use the time of the House in the most efficient way possible. The full text of my original speech will, however, be made available to hon. members and others, and I hope it will be read with some attention.
If in speaking today I convince some hon. members-and I am especially thinking of the almost 60 members who have not participated in a debate on this subject before- that we must look at this matter from a new perspective, then I will have done much to get this debate off to a good start.
I am convinced that if we attack this question objectively, then we must, from a logical, ethical and public policy point of view, conclude that capital punishment must be abolished once and for all.
In my view there are two central themes and two general lines of argument which embrace all of the secondary questions which must be answered in this debate. The first central theme concerns the issue of deterrence or, more broadly put, the question of how we can effectively protect the Canadian public against violent crime, in this case, murder. It is a discussion of the means to accomplish the end, which is protection.
I should like to go through the argument with regard to deterrence and protection step by step because in my view an examination of the evidence must lead us to the conclusion that capital punishment is no more effective a means of protecting society than other alternative less severe and less error prone means.
The second general line of argument concerns goals. While it is often said that arguments concerning means and arguments concerning ends or values are wholly distinct kinds of arguments, I feel that each has something to

add to the other. I am convinced that many of those debating the question of capital punishment focus too narrowly, and for that reason misconstrue the nature of our task in this debate.
There is no doubt that those opposing the abolition of capital punishment will cite statistics to show that the reported murder rate in Canada has climbed since the last executions were carried out in 1962 from 1.2 murders per 100,000 population to 2.4 murders per 100,000 population in 1974. This is a legitimate statistic to cite, but the conclusion drawn from it is often based on such a narrow view of the problem we are confronted with as to make that conclusion suspect.
Those citing the increase in the murder rate and concluding that the lack of executions in Canada since 1962 explains the increase in murders delude themselves and those who listen to them. I say this because this argument utterly ignores the dimensions of the problem of violent crime. This lack of perspective, and this facile assignment of cause and effect relationship between the lack of executions as cause and the rise in the murder rate as effect are a principal stumbling block to an intelligent and informed public discussion of the real problem.
I can demonstrate to hon. members that the real problem we must deal with is not simply one of murder here in Canada but that of crime throughout the western world. In my original text I give statistics and arguments to support that demonstration. I do not, I hasten to add, point this out with a view to sloughing off responsibility or minimizing the horror of murder. Far from it. I do so only in order to point out that we must address ourselves to the right questions and that a simple concentration on capital punishment and murder takes much too restricted a view of the questions about which Canadians are concerned.
Concentration on the issue of capital punishment does not serve us well if our purpose is, as it should be, the finding of truly effective means of protecting the public against violent crime. Such a concentration serves instead to distract our efforts, as was pointed out by Sir Robert Mark, a 38-year veteran and present commissioner of the London Metropolitan Police, better known as Scotland Yard. This distinguished spokesman for the police community in Great Britain, in addressing the Canadian Association of Chiefs of Police in Canada last summer made precisely this point. He said:
I am therefore opposed to the death penalty and so are most of my senior and most experienced colleagues, simply because its continuance prevents the reforms necessary to increase the effectiveness of criminal justice.
In presenting the peace and security program the government is focusing on these real problems and this focus aims at including only effective measures to protect the public and excluding ineffective measures. That is why we are now debating this bill to abolish capital punishment.
Having said this, I should like once more to come back to the two principal questions I set out a few moments ago on the specific question of capital punishment: the question of whether capital punishment is an effective means to the end of protecting the public, and the question of whether
May 3, 1976

the use of capital punishment is in keeping with the end or values which we as a society embrace.
The question of means boils down in essence to a question of effectiveness. The essential question is not whether the death penalty deters any would be murderers but whether it deters them more than life imprisonment does. As Professor James Q. Wilson of Harvard puts this issue:
It is a matter of dispute whether any penalty will have a deterrent effect on murderers, but surely the prospect of a long prison term will have as much as most others. For the death penalty to be warranted, it would have to supply an additional increment of deterrence sufficient to offset the costs of imposing it, those costs being the risk of executing an innocent man, the opportunities for discrimination in imposing the penalty, and the foregone possibility of rehabilitating the murderer. Fairness would always be a problem .. . because, though imposition of the death penalty could be made mandatory, juries in such cases might be unwilling to convict at all for fear of convicting wrongly.
If this is the question, Mr. Speaker, what is the answer? From all the studies that have been done, both here in Canada and in other nations, one cannot draw the conclusion that the prospect of capital punishment is a more effective deterrent to prospective murderers than is the prospect of life imprisonment. Hon. members need not take my word for it. Let me refer to other authors more expert in the field than I am whose conclusions, I think, hon. members should listen to with close attention.
If I had time this evening I would cite at some length the conclusions of Professor Thorsten Sellin who showed that capital punishment has no unique effect as between abolitionist and retentionist states over time, and as it especially affected the safety of policemen and prison guards. For a fuller examination of these points I would refer hon. members to the speech I gave on capital punishment three years ago and again to the original text of the speech I was to give here tonight.
Professor Sellin's findings were also supported by many other researchers. This evening I will cite only one of them who carried out research on the subject of deterrents in the Canadian context.
Professor Fattah's findings played an important role in the last debate on this subject and are worth referring to again by those who have not read them recently. The conclusion of the study on the deterrent effects of capital punishment in the Canadian context is that homicide rates are conditional on factors other than the death penalty. They suggest that the cause of homicide and murder cannot be found in any single factor but in a total social situation in which a specially important or particular punishment can have little or no effect. Professor Fattah concluded that:
The suspension (of the death penalty) is unlikely to have played a part in the ... light increase in the homicide rate in recent years ...
These conclusions of three years ago are equally supportable now, on the basis of later data. In 1973 as compared to 1972 the murder rate in Montreal and Vancouver fell and the murder rate in Toronto rose. The 1974 figures as compared to 1973 show a reversal of this: that is, the murder rate in Montreal and Vancouver rose, while that in Toronto fell. In 1974 as compared to 1973 the murder rate in Canada dropped in four provinces and rose in all the others.
Since the same law, with the same penalty, is in effect in all parts of Canada, then clearly the variation in rates of crime cannot be explained solely by that sanction. Other
Capital Punishment
factors are at work, and if we are to do anything effective about violent crime then we must focus on those other factors rather than on the illusionary effect of the statute and the penalty itself.
While I am on this topic I should like to address the question raised by the findings of the Econometric School of Deterrence and, specifically, the findings of Professor Ehrlich of the University of Chicago. In a widely cited article Professor Ehrlich's sophisticated statistical studies are purported to show that each additional execution would have resulted in seven or eight fewer murders. Because the results of Professor Ehrlich's analysis differ markedly from the results of previous research on this question, his work has naturally been very closely examined by a large number of scholars representing a variety of academic disciplines.
Robert G. Hann, in a detailed analysis of the Ehrlich study and the follow-up studies resulting from it, stresses the finding of Professor Friedman of Berkeley University, whose examination of Ehrlich's work led him to the startling conclusion that if an algebraic error committed by Ehrlich himself were corrected and if the other aspects of his work were valid, then Ehrlich's own analysis would imply that each execution is related to an increase of 14 murders, rather than a decrease of seven or eight. I cite these studies because it is important to recognize that those who would cite Professor Ehrlich without at the same time citing those who feel his study is fatally flawed by methodological and statistical errors are treading on very shaky ground.
What is it possible to conclude from all of these studies on the deterrent effect of capital punishment? It is my contention that if no irrefutable evidence can be brought forward that capital punishment is a more effective deterrent to the commission of murder than is a lengthy sentence, then we must conclude that a lengthy sentence is preferable, and that the burden of proof to conclude otherwise rests with those favouring the death penalty.

speechtext: Why?

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURK RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Because you are taking life when you propose the death penalty. The burden of proof is on those who propose retention of the death penalty. They must show that retention does some good in society and has positive effect. Furthermore, I do not think retentionists can logically or ethically discharge that burden of proof.
But in saying this I am moving into the second question of major importance, the question of whether the death penalty can be supported by moral arguments, which is to say, by arguments setting out to show that capital punishment is the only adequate punishment to express society's outrage against the murderer. On the one side of this question are the many Canadians who would reject the death penalty even if it could be proven to have a significant effect in furthering the end of protecting Canadian society against murder and other violent crime. One of the most moving statements of this nature I have ever heard was written by Mrs. Pauline Maitland whose husband, Constable Leslie Maitland, was murdered in Toronto by a

May 3, 1976
Capital Punishment
man who currently awaits our decision on death row. Mrs. Maitland wrote as follows:
In no way do I wish to interfere with the course of justice and the safety of an already overworked police department, but the killing of this man would be completely foreign to all the moral standards of both my late husband and myself ... It would not bring Leslie back and it is too easy a way out for all of us. Society condemns murder, but is willing to accept the murder of this man, in the name of justice. Please do what you can to prevent this terrible second crime, before it is too late.
On the other side of this question are those who believe that it is a dishonour to the victim of murder to do other than put to death his murderer, quite aside from the possible deterrent effect on others.
There is little that argument can do to affect those who hold either absolute view. But, despite this, I do think it is reasonable to say that the vast majority of Canadians hold views on the question of the suitability of capital punishment in our society that are amenable to factual and reasoned argument, and are not based on either absolutist moral position. It is these people I am addressing this evening.
To begin with, then, let us try to define the argument that capital punishment is the only "just" or "fitting" penalty for murder a little more closely. Clearly those who call for the reinstatement of capital punishment in order adequately to satisfy society's justified condemnation of the murderer are not setting up the death penalty itself as a goal or a value for society. I am sure that those who argue this position take it up because they see capital punishment as a justified reaction, not as an end in itself. But if it is not an end in itself, what then is it? Clearly, then, it is a means to another end, and that other end is the effective protection of society and the righteous expression of society's outrage against those who violate the ultimate value of the right to live peaceful and safe lives. But just as clearly the moral discussion on this point must then centre around the question of whether capital punishment is in fact just and fair both in theory and in application.
This is a complex argument, and because of time restrictions I must leave out some parts which are included in my original text. In the first place there is a great deal of evidence that, if justice requires fairness in application, then application of capital punishment in the past has not been just, because it has been applied disproportionately to those who are poor, unrepresented, and members of minority groups. This is a fact that is well established and does not merely refer to the contentious issue of execution in error alone.
Second, the sanction of death cannot be considered merely a quantitative extension of other sanctions in our criminal law. It is qualitatively, fundamentally, irretrievably different in kind and, as such, we as policy makers and as citizens bear an especially heavy burden to show that the special disadvantages which accompany the use of capital punishment outweigh the need to demonstrate society's outrage against murderers by other, less severe means.
What are some of these special disadvantages which accompany the use of the death penalty? I have very briefly referred to the irreversibility of the act of execution, which sets the death penalty in a separate category apart from all other penalties. I have also referred briefly to the possibility of execution in error, and to the inevita-

bility-according to Professor Charles Black of the Yale Law School-of execution as a result of the application of capricious, arbitrary, and therefore discriminatory standards. Another argument frequently brought up in this connection is that juries are more reluctant to convict when the life of the defendant is at stake than when the penalty is one of fine or imprisonment. Do we have evidence to support this contention? The answer in Canada is yes, we do.
In the eight decades between 1880 and 1960 the average yearly conviction rate in Canada for murder was 37.7 per cent, whereas for manslaughter it was 49.7 per cent, for attempted murder 51.6 per cent, for shooting and wounding 64.6 per cent. A study of these figures, and of the figures between 1961 and 1974 showing that three out of five of those charged with capital murder were convicted of a lesser offence, makes it possible to infer that Canadian jurors are loath to convict for capital murder, but are quite prepared to convict for a lesser offence where life is not at stake.
From another point of view Professor Wilson takes note of the interesting fact that:
In Great Britain, where judges had less discretion in imposing the death penalty than they do in the United States, the number of murderers found insane-and so spared the gallows-dropped sharply after the death penalty was abolished in 1965. It is hard to believe that there were fewer insane persons in Britain after abolition of the death penalty; what apparently happened was that the authorities no longer felt that it was necessary to protect the accused from penalties when the penalty was no longer death.
There is one final set of facts which I wish to bring to the attention of hon. members in order to allow them to weigh more adequately the wisdom of approving the death penalty as a justifiable penalty for murder. A recent article by Daniel Glaser and Max Zeigler showed that those who would have us indulge in the violence of state-sanctioned executions would do so only at the cost of engendering more violence-more murder-in our society. Glaser and Zeigler wrote:
Demands that capital punishment be restored are raised whenever the public is outraged at a particularly heinous and highly publicized killing, but the geographic facts presented here suggest that this 'gut response' is counter-productive as a means of reducing the prevalence of murder. The evidence shows that where use of the death penalty is most frequent there is less long-run outrage against killers than prevails in states that forbid murder, whether by private parties or by the government. The alternatives to violence are, in addition to a respect for the sacredness of life, the many civilized procedures and practices of analysing, negotiating, legally adjudicating, or simply tolerating disagreements. All of these alternatives are impaired or impeded rather than nurtured when the government resorts to the murderer's methods.
If this conclusion is correct, that the carrying out of executions by the state not only does not prevent murders but actually may serve to create or maintain a climate where more murders and more violence exists, then the argument that the death penalty is a just and fitting punishment in our society in order to show our outrage against murder must be seen to be empty and dangerous rhetoric.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would also like to say a few words to those who might be inclined to oppose this bill on the grounds that it is not a perfect piece of legislation, or on the grounds that the alternative suggested in
May 3, 1976

the bill is not precisely the alternative they would like to see.
First, I am not arguing that this bill is perfect, or that in proposing this bill we are offering a guarantee that there will be no more murders in Canada. To those who have doubts about this bill because they think that abolition is right but the proposed alternative is not, I would sound a note of caution. The Canadian public are concerned about crime and have a right to expect protection. Murder is a horrible and heinous crime and must be sanctioned severely if we are adequately to express society's denunciation of the murderer.
I disagree with those who argue that a life sentence with no parole eligibility for 25 years is worse than death. A period of incarceration, with hope of parole, and with the built-in additional incentive for the inmate, and protection for the guards, of a review of that parole eligibility after 15 years is necessarily better than a sentence of death because it removes the possibility of an irreversible error of execution.
Second, available studies, including those carried out by Joseph Vernet, S.J., provide no evidence that life imprisonment is as cruel or more cruel than is execution. His survey of European countries which have abolished the death penalty in order to ascertain whether this abolition gave rise to more cases of insanity, premature death, suicide, escape attempts, and frequent punishment among those sentenced to lengthy periods of incarceration, provided no evidence to support this proposition.
Furthermore, the government has committed itself as part of the peace and security package to improving general conditions within institutions through such measures as greater flexibility of institutional assignment in smaller and more specialized institutional centres, greater efforts toward staff training and improved deployment of staff resources in such programs as the team concept and living unit concept, new programs for training and work assignments for inmates, the completion of the five regional psychiatric centres, and a great deal of research to identify the effects of long-term incarceration and other related factors.
Some hon. members might cite their constituents as saying this sort of program costs too much and that the taxpayers do not want to bear the burden of paying approximately $14,000 per year per capital murderer over the term of a long sentence. To those who are unwilling to pay the costs of incarcerating these people and who wish to save money by carrying out executions, I would like to say the following in reply.
First, I am certain that no hon. member would agree that human life should be expended because of potential monetary savings alone. That is a principle which I am sure no serious person would argue.
Second, the whole argument is based upon a fallacy. If we were to execute the 11 people currently on death row we would not be saving $14,000 a year for each of those inmates for each year he is kept in prison. This is because the cost of maintaining the inmate is arrived at by dividing the total number of inmates into the total cost of running our institutions, and the marginal difference of eliminating 11 inmates would be so miniscule as to make practical-
Capital Punishment
ly no difference whatsoever in the over-all cost of running our system.
One recent estimate of the marginal cost of keeping one more inmate in our federal penitentiaries worked out the additional cost for food, clothing, sanitary supplies and daily wages at just over $3.50 per day. This marginal cost may even be less than the special costs of trying, appealing, detaining under special guard and executing those found guilty of capital murder, as was suggested before the United States Senate committee on the death penalty and by such authorities as the late Governor Winthrop Rockefeller of Arkansas and former Governor Pat Brown of California.
I have argued today that there are two major themes of debate on the subject of capital punishment: the first is an argument over means, the second over values. I have examined briefly each of the attendant arguments on these two major themes and would refer hon. members to my full text for a more detailed examination of the arguments involved.
As a result of these arguments I am convinced that hon. members will see that the retention of capital punishment is not only ineffective but that it may actually be counter productive to the goal of protecting the Canadian public against murder.
When we examine the question objectively, and when we study the evidence closely, logically, and with an open mind, then the conclusion we must reach, if we are to discharge our responsibility to the Canadian people as legislators of sound and effective laws, is that capital punishment must be abolished in Canada now, and that this bill should be passed.

My speech is going to be brief, as my speeches usually are in this House.
I am a retentionist and will be voting against the bill. I want to make clear at the outset that I, as with other members of this party, will be speaking for myself. All members in this party who will be participating in this debate will be speaking their own minds and will be voting as they see fit.

I have no doubt that that one particular vote is going to be free; none at all.
The Solicitor General will, I am sure, review the statistics, as no doubt other members intend to do. In my opinion that is a useless basis for argument. I do not think any more can be said than has been said in the three previous debates on this subject. Nonetheless I do not endorse the point of view expressed in one of the newspaper editorials tonight-I believe it was in the Ottawa Citizen-that closure should be imposed; that was the course this newspaper advocated on the ground that everything has been said which could possibly be said and therefore we should vote and get on with it. I happen to agree with the latter part of the suggestion, but I also believe members should have an opportunity to speak. However, those speeches, I believe, should be brief so that we need not be here until mid-July or mid-August.
No doubt those responsible for government strategy had the vacation in mind when they put the bill before us at this time. Speeches should be kept brief for that simple reason.
One can use the statistics the Solicitor General has exposed tonight to support an argument either for or against the retention of capital punishment. I do not intend to deal with those statistics but I am going to maintain that the death penalty is a deterrent. Obviously the government does not share that view, although I am sure the vast majority of the people of Canada do share it. The most recent polls certainly seem to support that contention.
I certainly do not put down the vast majority of Canadian public opinion as the Solicitor General attempted to do tonight, by inference if not directly, as being illogical or ill-reasoned, or opinion which is the product of closed minds. Simply because our opinion does not agree with his does not mean it is illogical, it does not mean that it has been reached with a closed mind, or that it has been formed by bias or prejudice on one side.

I will accept that statement, but the hon. gentleman did generalize by referring to "those on the other side of the argument", which includes that segment of the public which holds differing views.
My belief that the death penalty is a deterrent has its roots in my early experience in the Armed Forces. There are not too many of us left in this House who served in World War II. And there are not many of us, if any, who were not scared proverbially every time we came face to face with situations in that war which might cause death. In my activities, as someone required to fly over enemy territory and shoot and drop bombs and so on, there was never a moment when death was not a constant companion or when I was not frightened of meeting the spectre of death. I maintain that every one of us, or at least every
May 3, 1976

normal one of us-I do not know how many that eliminates on the other side-would react in the same way.
There is not one normal human being on the face of the earth who does not fear death. I do not believe this can be gainsaid. One is therefore led to the conclusion, probably over-simplistic, that death must be a deterrent. No one is going to attempt to cross the tracks at a subway station if he sees a train is coming. No one is going to open the door of an aircraft flying at 30,000 feet if he believes that by so doing he is bound to fall out. No one would do a rash, foolish act if they thought death would result.
It may be that because medicine and law stand widely apart these days the provisions of the Criminal Code do not adequately provide for the treatment of those who commit murder, of those who are not absolutely normal. I am speaking of the legal definition of insanity and the medical definition of insanity. Perhaps they should be brought closer together, but that is another matter. However, it seems to me there are a large number of murders committed by persons who, even medical science would agree, are normal but for the commission of the crime of murder on their part. To them I say the death penalty is a deterrent.
I know the government does not believe this for a number of reasons, one being its recent rejection of the bill of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) respecting the carrying of firearms. The right hon. gentleman by his bill, which is on the order paper, wants a mandatory five year term imposed on any person caught with a firearm in his possession during the commission of a criminal offence. I say that is a deterrent. Before individuals commit a crime with a firearm in their possession I suggest they will think twice, knowing that if they are caught they will serve an additional five years in prison on conviction, quite apart from the sentence imposed on them for committing the actual crime.
It may be over-simplistic, Mr. Speaker, but I also believe that people will think twice about committing murder if they know that on conviction the death penalty awaits them. That is the conclusion I have reached, and I have not been swayed otherwise by the last debate on capital punishment or the two previous debates through which I have sat and listened to all the statistics and arguments pro and con.
The Solicitor General says that an examination of the evidence-and I am sure he has read volumes of it-reveals that capital punishment is no more effective than other means in deterring crime. One can cite the same statistics and adopt the same philosophy for saying that an examination of the evidence reveals there is no other more effective method of deterring murder than capital punishment. You can go around in an ever-repetitive circle in the statistical argument.
I believe my argument may be best summed up for the most part by a letter that I received very recently in the mail, as did all hon. members, from a Vancouver solicitor in connection with the recent murder there of Doreen Garbutt. He writes as of April 7 last:
At this most important time in the parliamentary debate concerning amendment to the criminal law and, seemingly incidentally, concerning
Capital Punishment
capital punishment, I thought you might wish to consider the recent murder of Doreen Garbutt in Vancouver.
Doreen had risen to be office manager in a local company and was indeed a very charming, intelligent, hardworking woman who participated actively in voluntary community affairs. My wife and I considered her to be a most delightful friend as did the hundreds of others who attended her funeral.
One day, a few weeks ago, a former employee of Doreen's employer, who had been fired and who had threatened the employer, brought a rifle-
In my own parenthesis I say not a "handgun".
-into Doreen's office and killed her instantly in her chair. So much for a meaningful, worthwhile 35 year old; death instantly, at the hands of a man who then said; "that's my kind of justice".
This murderer will receive all the protection and help that our law has provided. He will be treated politely, will be well fed, well housed, given psychiatric examination and help, should he need it, and will be provided with competent counsel. He may then be convicted and jailed after which he will probably be paroled.
Even with our law as it is, this murderer could never be executed. Even with our law as it is, no murderer is executed in Canada because our federal cabinet abuses at least the intent of the law and commutes every sentence of death. The cabinet does not follow the law-it willfully disregards the law and for individual, personal reasons, collectively applied, it refuses execution for all convicted murderers.
Again I say in parenthesis, as it has been doing for the last seven to nine years.
And so it is that a bill is now before parliament which is not a "free" vote with respect to capital punishment because the issue of capital punishment is protectively cloaked in deliberate confusion by that same cabinet which ignores the law today.
I do not wish to make Doreen Garbutt a martyr to any cause, I do not believe she would wish to be. I do wish to point out that any person who has killed any other and who has been given the protection of the police and judicial systems which Canadians previously enjoyed and who is then determined sane and then on final court appeal, found guilty of that killing, has received every reasonable human and humane consideration.
It is my opinion that the convicted killer should then be put to death. I do not approve of hanging because I believe it to be unnecessarily cruel-the least cruel, least sensational, method of all should be used.
You may, or may not, agree with my opinion but at least I can speak freely. You, as a representative of your constituents, do not have the freedom I have because the bill ties your hands. It has been seen fit to present a bill to you which refuses you the "free" vote promised.
I urge you to defeat the bill presently before you and require the government to provide you with an opportunity for a truly "free" vote on capital punishment. At that same time, by additional legislation, the permissiveness now so evident in our criminal law could be restrained.
I might close on that note, Mr. Speaker. How does the cabinet, let alone the Solicitor General, expect me to lend credibility to his argument when he and his colleagues in cabinet have for so many years been willfully disregarding the law which they themselves presented to parliament and provided the majority for its passage?

If the hon. member holds the opposite view, I respect absolutely that view. I do not wish to become involved in an emotional partisan split here in this debate. However, there are those of us who believe the death penalty should be retained, just as there are others who believe, just as deeply and just as sincerely, that it should be abolished. I am simply stating the reasons why I believe it should be retained.
I believe the death penalty is a deterrent. I have no knowledge to believe it is not. It seems logical to me that, since every human being has a fear of death, if this is on the law books it will make a person think twice before planning to kill someone deliberately. The statistics really are not convincing to me. They can be used either way.

Having said, and having promised the House, that I would be brief, I shall resume my seat after once again emphasizing the fact that those who follow me in this debate from this party will be speaking from the depths of their convictions on a personal basis and not on a party basis. That is the way the vote will go over here. I would hope there will be a change on the opposite side from the previous situation. I would hope hon. members opposite will swallow their ambition and vote from their beliefs at this one time and freely express their opinions.
