speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I share one thing with the last speaker, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). This is the fourth debate in which I have participated on this subject of capital punishment. Having agreed with him that far, may I say I agree with very little else he said.
There is, of course, a danger of repetition. It is reasonable also to anticipate that in a matter of such emotional content it will be difficult to imagine that the attitudes of members will be much changed by the speeches made in this House. Nevertheless it is one of the most solemn obligations we have as members of parliament to deal with this issue as wisely as we know how.
In my party we agreed with the view that the subject matter, being clearly one of principle, members should be permitted to vote freely according to their consciences. It is nevertheless a fact that a common approach among the members of my party has brought all members of our party to the same view, namely, that we should vote for the bill and in favour of ending capital punishment.
In this debate I shall be speaking for myself, and other members of my party will be speaking for themselves. We understand why there are so many in society who believe that capital punishment is a necessary protection for human life and who believe, however unpalatable it may be, that the state should deliberately take the lives of individuals, and that this must be done in order to protect society. If we believed that society could be so protected we would have to support capital punishment; but after the closest and most careful study we are satisfied that capital punishment does not discourage crime nor is it the most effective deterrent. If it is not an effective deterrent, there is no excuse for it.
We reject the view that the state should impose capital punishment to satisfy public demand for vengeance. It is perfectly true that the death penalty may deter some. It is equally clear that life imprisonment may deter some. The facts on record are beyond dispute that on balance the death penalty does not perform the function its supporters claim.
A British royal commission on capital punishment noted that a study from many countries showed there was no definite evidence that the abolition of capital punishment led to an increase in the murder rate. Studies have been made in neighbouring states of the United States of a somewhat similar nature. Some of these states had abolished capital punishment and some had not. Similar studies were made of states and provinces in Australia. A study was made in two adjoining provinces, one of which had abolished capital punishment and the other which had not. All these studies indicated that the rise and fall of the
May 3, 1976

murder rate were just about the same in the states which had abolished capital punishment as in those which had not. So the death penalty was not a determining factor.
Two eminent penologists, Barnes and Teeters, in the book "New Horizons in Criminology", state:
History reveals the most varied and numerous proofs-
I underline the word "proofs".
-that there is no correlation between the severity of the criminal code and the infrequency of crime. The statistics which we have available show that there is no ground whatever for holding that the murder rate increases when the death penalty is abolished.
Canadian studies have produced precisely the same conclusion.
The chairman of the British commission, Sir Ernest Gowers, was originally a supporter of capital punishment, but after presiding over the commission for four years and hearing expert witnesses, he became an abolitionist. He referred to the situation in Belgium where the results were so conclusive that further argument has been silenced and the lesson seems to have been learned, he said, that the best way to have respect for human life is to refrain from taking it in the name of the law.
Sweden formally abolished capital punishment in 1902, and I believe has one of the lowest murder rates in the world. It has one of the lowest rates of homicide of any country in the world. I was speaking to Swedish members of parliament and they told me there is no pressure whatever to reinstate capital punishment in that country.
[DOT] <2110)
Many hon. members here may recall that in the past in Canada the crime of rape was a criminal offence. The death penalty was abolished in Canada in April, 1955, and the maximum penalty of life imprisonment was substituted for it. Since that day there has been a steady fall in the convictions for that offence. Once again it is perfectly obvious that the death penalty was not an effective deterrent. Are we to ignore these facts, or should we take facts into account in making our judgment on this solemn matter? I suggest that we are obliged by conscience and common sense to have regard to the clear facts of the situation.
It was almost 13 years ago that the British House of Commons declared by a majority vote that the death penalty for murder no longer accords with the true needs or interests of a civilized society. One could go on and on with statistics, but the picture is indeed clear enough.
There is one aspect of the matter which should not be overlooked. I think the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) mentioned it. I have and I retain a deep respect for the administration of justice in Canada, and believe that it is of the utmost importance to the maintenance of law and order in a decent society that we should respect the law and those who are appointed to administer it. But this does not mean that there is not a real possibility of error. The courts themselves can make mistakes and sometimes make them.
Indeed, as one who practised before the courts for nearly 40 years, I personally know of cases in which the courts did in fact make mistakes. One of the best known cases was in England, the Christie case, where a man was executed
Capital Punishment
after having been found guilty of murder, and only some years later did the person who committed the crime admit his guilt and demonstrate beyond doubt that the court had erred. There is a finalty about the death penalty which makes it impossible to correct such errors.
I was very familiar with the case of Steven Truscott who escaped capital punishment when he was found guilty of murder only because he was 14 or 15 years of age. I followed that case closely, and in my belief the dissenting judgment of Mr. Justice Hall in the Supreme Court of Canada was correct and the majority judgment of that court was wrong. Perhaps my judgment is wrong in respect of this case, but the possibility of error is very real and it is inconsistent with capital punishment.
The Solicitor General has already referred to P. C. Leslie Maitland who in 1973 was shot and died. He was a constituent of mine, and so is his wife. Naturally there was great indignation about the murder for he was a very fine police officer. I have received, and handed to the Solicitor General, a letter from Mrs. Maitland who now resides in Scotland. I have a slightly fuller version of the letter than the one which the Solicitor General read to the House. I have her permission to quote the letter, which reads as follows: Dear Mr. Brewin:
I learned from my brother-in-law that the man who killed my husband P. C. Leslie Maitland last February 1st, has now been sentenced to death. I would like you to know that the views of myself and my husband's family, on capital punishment, remain unchanged. We are totally against it. It would not bring Leslie back and it is too easy a way out for all of us. Society condemns murder, but is willing to accept the murder of this man, in the name of justice. Please do what you can to prevent this terrible second crime, before it is too late. Abolitionists may be in the minority but we still have the right to be heard. You can count on me, and my family to do anything possible to help. In no way do I wish to interfere with the course of justice and the safety of an already overworked police department, but the killing of this man would be completely foreign to all the moral standards of both my late husband and myself.
I have received, and I am sure all other members have, a number of messages from constituents, some for and some against capital punishment, but frankly I regard Mrs. Maitland's letter as one of the most cogent influences on my decision.
I want to mention another matter. Quite a few of the letters I have received have invoked religion and the Bible in support of capital punishment. The fact of the matter is, however, that nearly all the major churches have clearly and emphatically repudiated capital punishment. Included in these are the Roman Catholic church, or at least many of its spokesmen, the Anglican, Presbyterian, United, Baptist and Mennonite churches, and many others such as the Society of Friends.
I believe that the ancient precepts in the Old Testament which are quoted as supporting capital punishment were written when a barbaric system prevailed. Indeed the writers of those words were progressive. They sought to restrict the desire for vengeance to the person responsible for some crime and not invoke it and promote feuds between warring families. But they did not confine the notion of capital punishment to murder, nor did they confine the passage in the Bible in which they referred to murder but included such offences as cursing one's parents, trespassing on a neighbour, adultery, and other such

May 3, 1976

Capital Punishment
offences. Can it be seriously urged that we go back to those barbaric days?
For me the basic Christian message is contained in the spirit of compassion and mercy with which Christ treated the crime of adultery. When a woman who was clearly guilty of adultery was being stoned by her accusers, Christ said, "Let him who is without sin cast the first stone". In my view this represents the voice of true religion.
All I can say to those who have written and urged me in the name of Christianity to support capital punishment is that I think they are wrong. I do not say this arrogantly but with a clear conviction. I have also received letters from social workers, and they too have expressed the view that capital punishment should be abolished.
I am well aware of the fact that as a general rule policemen are of the opinion that capital punishment protects them. But this is not a universal view. The Solicitor General has already mentioned Sir Robert Mark, the head of Scotland Yard, who in a statement published in the Globe and Mail on August 29 of last year called for the abolition of the death penalty.
As I am sure all other members of the House do, I respect the important function that the police have in the protection of society. Nevertheless I think many people are in danger of expecting police to fulfil a function which they are not trained or obliged to fulfil in society, that is, to make the laws. In a democratic society it is the elected members of parliament who make the laws, not policemen. We should, of course, listen to what policemen have to say, but we should not permit ourselves to accept their views automatically as to what the law should be. Their function is to enforce the law, and in my view an effective enforcement of the law, the adequate training and payment of the police, would be a more adequate protection for society than capital punishment could ever be. I do not believe that capital punishment is an effective protection for society.
I want to deal now with a matter which has been discussed, and that is the position that members of parliament should take on this issue in respect of opinions expressed to them by constituents. It is sometimes said, by means of consultation of polls, that a majority of people in a particular riding, or in Canada as a whole, favour capital punishment, and therefore it is the duty of a member of parliament to reflect this opinion. I reject this argument. It is contrary to the principles of parliamentary democracy.
Of course any sensible member of parliament and one who expects to be re-elected considers his constituents' views and is sensitive to their opinions. However, we were not elected to be computers who count heads. We were elected to use our own judgment and conscience in the interest of the society we represent. We have no right, in my opinion, to put that responsibility off or to yield to what may be a temporary majority, or indeed may not be a majority.
I have received letters on both sides of the question from my constituents, and I think they are fairly evenly balanced. However, in the ultimate analysis I must vote in accordance with my own conviction of what is right or wrong. If enough of my constituents reject my view, they

can defeat me in an election, but they have no right to stifle my own conscience or principles. If we were all to adopt this philosophy-that it is the majority view in a constituency, when one does not know exactly how to determine, which should dictate our opinions and actions in the House-we would deprive the House of members of independence of character who are required for the job.
I have stated this clearly and can only add that this view of the functions of a member of parliament has been clearly expressed many times before. As far as I know the first expression was by the famous Conservative writer, Edmund Burke. The same opinion was expressed by Winston Churchill, and if one comes closer to home, by the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. I am not ashamed to follow in their tradition, which I think is the true parliamentary tradition.
I regret that so many people in our society misunderstand and think that they have the right, because they believe they have a majority, to decide how we should vote. Quite recently the British House of Commons voted almost overwhelmingly for the continuing abolition of capital punishment. This was contrary to the views said by the pollsters to represent majority opinion in Great Britain. If the elected members of the mother of parliaments have the guts to stick to their convictions, I believe we in Canada should follow their example.
I should like to close with two or three quotations. The first is from the great Archbishop Temple, Archbishop of Canterbury, who said:
I believe that the example of the state taking life even when it does so in return for a life already taken does more to lower the value of human life for its citizens than the deterrent influence of this penalty can do to protect lives. In this way I believe that the main influence of the retention of the death penalty is rather to increase than diminish the numbers of murders.
I want to quote another person who has already been quoted by the Solicitor General, Professor Sellin, who indeed is a scholar and expert in this field. He said this:
I have attempted to show that as now used capital punishment performs none of the utilitarian functions claimed by its supporters, nor can it ever be made to serve such functions. It is an archaic custom dying out through the world and ought to disappear in any civilized country.
There is one other quotation I wish to give to the House. It is a fairly lengthy one. It is a quotation from the writer Albert Camus, a very famous French writer who won the Nobel prize. He wrote an article entitled "Reflections on the Guillotine". It is true he was referring to the guillotine and not hanging, but I do not think the distinction is a very real one. He wrote this:
Shortly before the war of 1914, an assassin whose crime was particularly repulsive (he had slaughtered a family of farmers, including the children) was condemned to death in Algiers. He was a farm worker who had killed in a sort of bloodthirsty frenzy but had aggravated his case by robbing his victims. The affair created a great stir. It was generally thought that decapitation was too mild a punishment for such a monster. This was the opinion, I have been told, of my father, who was especially aroused by the murder of the children. One of the few things I know about him, in any case, is that he wanted to witness the execution, for the first time in his life. He got up in the dark to go to the place of execution at the other end of town amid a great crowd of people. What he saw that morning he never told anyone. My mother relates merely that he came rushing home, his face distorted, refused to talk, lay down for a moment on the bed, and suddenly began to vomit. He had just discovered the reality hidden under the noble phrases with
May 3, 1976

which it was masked. Instead of thinking of the slaughtered children, he could think of nothing but that quivering body that had just been dropped onto a board to have its head cut off.
I should like to have read more, but I will not do so. I commend "Reflections on the Guillotine" by Albert Camus as a most valuable and extremely well written statement of the case.
I conclusion I wish to say that I like all hon. members of the House, am very proud to be a Canadian. I will be even more proud if we in parliament reject firmly the backward step which would be involved in the retention of capital punishment.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a moment earlier the speakers before me were saying that it was the fourth debate on capital punishment and I realized that they are older than I as I participate in the third debate on capital punishment which is the subject matter of Bill C-84, an Act to amend the Criminal Code.
In 1967, the Liberal government presented the first bill concerning the abolition of capital punishment for a five year period experiment. In 1973, the present Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) tabled Bill C-2 recommending a partial and temporary abolition for another five year period but this time, to innovate, there was an exception for murders of policemen and prison guards. The Solicitor General was probably not satisfied with the results as Statistics Canada showed that violent crimes had increased during that experimental period.
With Bill C-84 we are again discussing capital punishment for the third time in ten years but this time the Solicitor General forces more firmly upon us the view that he always had about capital punishment. He proceeded progressively but so imperturbably that if he were alone against a whole population his view would still triumph. This is why he has always refused to submit this question to a public referendum. The minister knows very well that 70 per cent of the people would oppose his old bill and he still knows today that 71 per cent of the people favour the death penalty as long as social security will not be better guaranteed by the Criminal Code. And what is even more surprising is that the Solicitor General pretends to be a democrat in a one way democracy directed from the top. Mr. Speaker, I call this dictatorship. In any case, the present minister lost all his credibility with the people as he never respected his own legislation of 1973.
While emphasizing in his own Bill C-2 that murderers of policemen and prison guards would be put to death, what did the Solicitor General do with all these murderers who ridiculed the act by killing a number of prison guards and policemen between 1967-72 and 1976? He himself commuted these sentences into life imprisonment. Such is the concrete result of efforts by all members here during the past years. If the minister had spent the same amount of energy on improving penitentiary system, my assurance is we would not be faced with such a prison record that is shameful for a nation as industrialized and technologically advanced as ours, because these institutions are much more in the nature of schools for crime than rehabilitation establishments. Therefore, I cannot approve the suggestion
Capital Punishment
by the minister, in Bill C-84, that capital punishment should be reduced to 25, 15 and even 10 years according to the criminal's classification. Certainly within a few years we will have to follow the United States. They are considering reestablishing capital punishment that has been abolished in a number of states.
Since the tree must be known by its fruit, we cannot expect anything better if the minister keeps his portfolio for the next five years. After the law providing for capital punishment has been ignored for the past years, in cases where prison guards and policemen have been murdered, what will happen now that the sentence will be reduced to 25 years imprisonment? Everyone knows perfectly well that if the minister ignored the former restrictions, he will ignore to a greater extent still the maximum penalty of 25 or even 10 years imprisonment for first and second degree murder. I am even amazed there is no reference in the bill now before us to a third degree murder, for which a decoration would be provided.
What is discouraging in this bill, as indeed in every other one, is the total lack of any reference to the murderers' victims. The minister commiserates with the unhappy murderers but he cannot spare a thought for the latters' victims. Mr. Speaker, when will we have members humane enough to look into that difficult problem, namely the future of the murderers' victims. I have always felt the essential purpose of a legislation was the adequate protection of the general public, to ensure a safer and therefore more humane social life. This assumes elimination of troublemakers, and if possible their rehabilitation, and the redress of first or second degree damage done by such trouble makers. Finally, we need an effective and permanent policy for the diehards, since in my view they are the worst kind of mental cases there are in our psychiatric wards, with that difference that the latter are not first degree murderers. Before going any further with parole provisions, we will have to consider total reform of our Criminal Code to include rehabilitation, help for crime victims and also greater rights to police officers.
As long as we persist in shutting up our criminals in the schools of crime that our prisons now are, whether it be for two, three, four or even six years, they will come out even more rebellious, and I would even say even more refined in their future actions.
Let us stop deluding ourselves, Mr. Speaker, and let us listen to the opinions of former convicts who, after their release, found themselves homeless, with no money, with the identity of a former convict. What can such a man do under the circumstances if not go back to his former profession?
If we want to really help the convicts, let us forget about Bill C-84 and introduce in the House another bill which will allow us to make our prisons and reformatories more humane. We should first of all select convicts according to their age, their offence and their social condition. For this, we should have appropriate facilities, and, even more important, qualified personnel, including doctors, psychiatrists, nurses and social counsellors, to bring the required help to all those who can be rehabilitated, and especially those who wish to get out of their abnormal situation.
It is certainly not by arresting a young man and putting him in a cell with habitual criminals that we shall reach

our common goal. A society is made up of many elements and all its members cannot be super-intelligent beings or angels. We must therefore take it as it is, and face reality.
It is certainly not by releasing someone who is not ready to reintegrate society that we can maintain peace. However, it is up to us parliamentarians to act on behalf of those who cannot express their opinions, that is the convicts themselves. Of course, there are some habitual criminals, but the very great majority can be rehabilitated if we bring them the help that they expect from us, the elected representatives of the people, and only from us, let us not forget it.
Prisons can be compared with psychiatric institutions, and this is why I firmly believe that a selection is necessary and that the people responsible must be given the necessary tools to operate a selection and give each individual a proper orientation. I have known some young people who went to prison for a small offence, or for a trivial slip, and who became then well-known bandits because of a penitentiary system which denies them any opportunity for rehabilitation.
Have we thought for one moment of this prisoner who is labelled as a bandit and who once was a little boy with very legitimate ambitions, like any other youth but for whom, during all his childhood and adolescence the streets were the only meeting place and who often had to look into garbage cans to find his food. One day, he decided to get out of his misery at all cost, even through illegal means since he already saw himself in an illegal situation. This adolescent had all the necessary qualities to become a leader, but because of the serious faults of our society, he became the leader of a gang. But is he really responsible for his situation? Whose fault is it, I ask you, hon. members, whose fault is it?
Conditional release is still mentioned in this bill, but in order to make it less accessible. With the experience of recent years, I do not call it conditional release, but "pro-tectional" release, because unless an external influence, whether political, financial or other, apart from a few exceptions those releases are empty words. And I will go further, Mr. Speaker. In most cases, who is released and from what? Inmates from a smaller prison are released to go in a wider prison, but all the more fatal because of their lack of preparation. As a result they will become recidivists, for they will still prefer the walls of their earlier prison to those of incomprehension. As to assistance for victims of criminals, I repeat, our present code does not provide anything for them. Nevertheless, if the government is responsible for the welfare of the inmates, it is all the more so for that of the victims of criminals.
For example, take a father who is shot during a hold up; what is to become of his wife and children? Their pictures are taken at the funeral home, in church, and even back home from the graveyard, and then great silence. Often the families get only the meagre social welfare benefits to replace the income of the family's breadwinner shot while protecting our nice society.
Each time I witness such incidents, I wonder, in all fairness, what we are doing here. What does social justice mean to us? Mr. Speaker, why do 90 per cent of the
(Mr. Gauthier (Roberval).]
policemen favour capital punishment? They do so for all the reasons I just mentioned, and also because policemen feel increasingly vulnerable in front of well armed criminals. Besides the risks they run with criminals, they always fear that their efforts be destroyed before the judges.
I would even say that in some cases policemen have two enemies; the first standing in front of them, namely the gangster, and the other behind him, the judge who is waiting for him. In this regard I note some of the weaknesses of the present Criminal Code, because of the restrictions it imposes on them, namely that they must warn the criminal before firing. In short, the killer must shoot first. The consequence is logical: the policemen get it first.
I personally witnessed trials which I found simply repulsive. While I was well aware of all the precautions taken by the police agents, throughout the trial one would have sworn the real gangsters were the policemen themselves. If it is their duty to see to it that the law is respected, then the judges should give them greater support in what often proves to be a thankless task. After all those considerations, I often wonder who the real criminals are: are they to be found at the top or the botton of the ladder?
If we could question every prisoner to find out what really happened, we would be surprised to find out that 90 per cent of them are in prison through society's fault, often because of some influence which is said to be unknown but that we all know full well, that of money which has forced those people to choose the less honest way out.
I certainly do not have the time to present a table of the serious faults of our society in arriving at our judicial system, nor do I have the time to go over all the arguments that were made in this House since 1967. Everyone knows quite well why we were against the previous bills and why we will be against Bill C-84. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) repeated tonight all the arguments we heard in the past 10 years, and I am sure that a month from now we will be able to make another volume similar to that of 1967 and that of 1965.
In all those arguments, one soon realizes that the Solicitor General has a fixed idea on the issue of capital punishment. Indeed, he will necessarily continue to use his right of veto on every future conviction, and continue to have it his own way. That is why I regret this absolutely useless discussion and we should let the Solicitor General of Canada continue to commute sentences, as he has already done, without asking for anybody's permission. When the Solicitor General talks about respecting life, did he only ask himself whether murderers ever thought about the nice theories advocated by the minister? We noticed in the inquiries into organized crime that the heads of criminal organizations have much more realistic principles than the present legislators. They have their own law, and that law is beyond appeal. You notice that gangsters do not play on words, as politicians who always fear public opinion do. They do what they think is best for their own society. So I say that if you want to fight those organizations you will not win by decorating their murderers. Let us not forget that the state is there to fully protect society, and nice speeches will not make our fellow citizens feel more secure.
May 3, 1976

Let us get down to the job of reforming our whole Criminal Code, and let us stop wasting time repeating 10 or 15 year old speeches. In the meantime, let us keep the principle of capital punishment, even if the Solicitor General has his mind set on commuting all sentences to at least reassure a bit our people who are waiting impatiently for something new in criminal legislation.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURK RESPECTING PUNISHMENT FOR MURDER AND OTHER SERIOUS OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the speech I made in the House on May 14, 1973, and the many memos and papers I prepared and distributed on the subject of capital punishment, I shall refrain from elaborating on any arguments with which I dealt in the past. My approach means that many substantive points relating to capital punishment per se will not be made in this particular speech. I have chosen, instead, to deal with six aspects of the problem relating to capital punishment and crime in Canada: first, the general attitude of the public toward violence; second, my general approach to peace and security; third, the exaggerated perception of violence in society and one of its primary causes; fourth, the facts relating to violent crime in Canada, as I have determined through research; fifth, the new peace and security package, and a critique on it; lastly, capital punishment itself, on which subject I intend to make a few remarks.
Events in the past few years have created a condition in which the public are demanding sterner measures for the prevention of crime and the retention of criminals. Public clamour for sterner measures is both understandable and justifiable. The public's clamour and concern stem largely from the following considerations, as I see them: a perceived increase in violent and other types of criminal activity; a feeling that the criminal law is too lax that the judicial system imposes too light a punishment for many crimes that our prisons are insecure that our parole system is too lax in granting paroles generally and that temporary leaves and day passes are abused that the government itself is hesitant if not downright opposed to implementing capital punishment even when it is on our law books and that there is too much consideration for the criminal and too little consideration for the victim and society as a whole.
There is a feeling that dangerous criminals are too readily released on bail. There is a feeling that more emphasis is given to the rehabilitation of criminals rather than the protection of society. There is a general rebellion against the permissive society that all of us have lived through since the end of World War II. My approach to the general disposition of society largely parallels the concerns as I perceive them to be.
I am convinced that the vast majority of Canadians want to be assured that they and their children will be safe on our streets and not become the victims of criminal activity. I am inclined to believe that what we really need is new and tougher legislation covering a broad range of criminal offences, not just murder. I think the public to some extent feel that capital punishment through some miraculous means will in fact achieve those objectives. There are others, and there are many parliamentarians among that group, who feel that in fact the retention of capital punish-
Capital Punishment
ment will not facilitate the return to a more peaceful and
secure society.
We must be assured that those who are imprisoned for criminal offences are held in institutions which are secure. That is self evident. We must also be assured that our parole boards do not grant temporary paroles or temporary leaves to prisoners if their release into society would pose a threat to the peace and security of the public at large.
We must take steps to guarantee that our law enforcement officers at every level are given adequate protection under the law and are provided with an appropriate legislative base so that they may perform their function of protecting society effectively.
We must ensure that our prisons are secure and that prison guards are given the maximum degree of protection in the performance of their dangerous work.
We must review our rehabilitation procedures so that the term of imprisonment itself will be conducive to rehabilitation. We must have special provision in the law to deal with the case of the "habitual criminal" so that such persons will not be released into society at the termination of a sentence if the court feels that they will constitute a continuing threat to the community as a whole.
The whole Criminal Code needs to be reviewed to ensure that penalties match the crime and to guarantee that sentences will be served so that we can maximize the deterrent effect of the criminal law. We need appropriate and reasonable control of firearms in our society so that we can minimize the incidents of their misuse. I have spoken more specifically on firearm control in a separate speech in the House of Commons and I will not go into detail on that today.
We require bail reform to ensure that bail is not granted to individuals whose release pending sentence would be a threat to society. We need to re-define first and second degree murder, and to increase substantially the pre-parole period for such offences. Police powers need to be substantially increased to assist them in successfully combating organized crime. In order to give more emphasis to crime prevention we need to broaden government activities by every level of government.
Efforts must be increased to identify the causes of alienation within our society which give rise to anti-social behaviour. Concentrated effort must be put forward to restore public confidence in the criminal law and its application through the courts and our law enforcement agencies. These and other things have to be done if we are to have a peaceful and secure society. However, governments and members of parliament must not only take into account the reality of the situation but also bear in mind the general attitude of our people.
Many Canadians are deeply disturbed by a persistent belief that their governments and institutions are "soft" on crime; there is a belief that there is more concern for the criminal than the victim. Neither of these beliefs are adequately based on fact. However, in a democratic free society the facts are almost irrelevant. The perception of the public is extremely important and governments and our institutions must behave in such a way as to restore their fundamental confidence.

May 3, 1976
Adjournment Debate
Aside from taking the measures already outlined, we must also take positive action to prevent the occurrence of crime. This is a very complex subject area and to deal with it we need to reconsider our present approach to education, mental health, recreational and employment opportunities, and a broad host of social measures. The conditions that give rise to young people turning to crime should be eliminated. The proposals for legislative change inherent in the preceding suggestions are reasonable but tough measures to provide greater security in our society. Such measures, however, will not satisfy everyone because some in our society have an exaggerated perception of the problem of violence in society. Radio, television, and the press have created in the minds of many a situation where they believe that there is more violence than actually exists.
A friend and constituent, Ann Farquhar, forwarded me the April, 1976, edition of Psychology Today. In that issue there was a research article dealing with violence on TV. The thrust of this article indicates that one of the more far-reaching effects of violence on television is to create a condition where people equate the violence they see on TV to the real world around them.
Violence on television thus has a two-fold effect. First, it suggests that violence is the appropriate and traditional means of settling disputes. Second, it creates in the heavy TV viewer a feeling that the world in reality is as violent as he sees it on television. This fear, the article indicates, may also bring increasing demands for police protection and election of law and order politicians. This has already happened.
I will continue later and call it ten o'clock now, Mr. Speaker.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF PLANNING FOR IMPROVED SURVEILLANCE, SEARCH AND RESCUE IN VIEW OF POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES
NATIONAL DEFENCE-REQUEST FOR DETAILS OF PLANNING FOR IMPROVED SURVEILLANCE, SEARCH AND RESCUE IN VIEW OF POSSIBLE EXTENSION OF JURISDICTION TO 200 MILES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question which I directed to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) on April 8 is important enough to take up a lot more time than that which is allotted tonight. The planning and implementation of a surveillance policy for Canada involves air-sea rescue and the patrol capability, not only to protect fishing vessels, but on a much broader base.
In his reply the minister stated that the imposition and extension of a 200 mile limit was hypothetical. However, he knows that Canada will declare either a 200 mile fisheries or economic zone and that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of State (Fisheries) (Mr. LeBlanc) must now be making
(Mr. Cafik.]
plans for such a course of action because there is little likelihood the Law of the Sea Conference now drawing to a close in New York will achieve international agreement.
The reason I continually raise the question of surveillance is because it appears that not too many appreciate the mission that Canada must undertake to provide a surveillance capacity and the enormous funding that will be required if one can imagine the area that will have to be patrolled. We must recognize the size of Canada, the length of its coastline, the massive extent of the part of the globe we occupy. We are far from ready to provide the surveillance which is required even though the minister has told us that the Department of National Defence plans to increase the amount of equipment available for this purpose.
Looking over the various departments concerned I find that the available strength is far below what is required. For example, the Canadian Coastguard Service operates 10 offshore cutters of between 70 feet and 224 feet, only one 33 foot shore based hovercraft, six 40-foot shore based launches, nine 15-foot inflatable inshore rescue boats, 14 44-foot lifeboats, and 33 helicopters which can respond only under ideal weather conditions. In addition, the Coastguard operates 65 other vessels with a secondary search and rescue role.
The Department of the Environment is increasing its inadequate patrol capability with a 205-foot helicopter-equipped patrol vessel, and two high speed aluminum patrol boats.
Moving to the navy, I feel I should quote from articles written by two of our learned retired admirals. This is what Vice-Admiral J. C. O'Brien had to say:
It is vital for us to invest in a strong navy with a realistic number of aircraft if we are to exhibit a real presence in all the ocean areas for which we consider ourselves responsible. I have always suggested a strong naval capability to at least 1500 miles off our coasts and this requires a much bigger effort than we are exerting now.
Clearly, we must have more ships. But the most direct way to meet this shortcoming initially would be to implement a composite plan involving a common fleet in which naval aircraft, support ships and destroyers would team up with a force of armed trawlers manned by a para-military reserve. This reserve would, I suggest, be directed by the navy because only the navy has the command and control facilities as well as the professional know-how to undertake the responsibility.
The writer goes on to recommend the formation of other para-military forces.
My second quotation is from an article by Rear-Admiral R. W. Timbrell who says:
For a number of years our government has expounded that both in the national and the world's interest our seabed out in the continental shelf or at least two hundred miles will be preserved and protected, and the point is rapidly approaching where this must be accepted either at this month's resumption of the Law of the Sea Conference (now taking place in New-York) or by unilateral action.
Such action will be meaningless unless we are prepared to provide a visible force of sufficient credibility in size and determination to enforce our declaration effectively. These forces will be required to patrol hundreds of thousands of square miles frequently and must be able to follow up immediately with on-the-spot investigation. The occasional patrol is clearly insufficient and of little value in view of the vastness of the area to be surveyed and the difficulties encountered in all the forms of weather to be found off Canada's seaboard. It would be simple, say, for a large group of foreign fishing trawlers with their
May 3, 1976

factory ships to move into a declared area, reap a harvest of fish in 12-24 hours and proceed outside the national limits without being spotted, let alone apprehended, unless we provide constant patrols and presence.
The time allotted to me does not allow me to refer to more examples. It is obvious that with the task force report due to surface by this summer, and following the recommendations from the Canadian Coastguard, there must be co-ordination of effort on the part of all. The report to which I have referred should be carefully considered by a joint committee at which time witnesses such as Rear-Admiral Timbrell and Vice-Admiral O'Brien should be heard. My colleague tells me that the Americans now have a contingency plan. We must plan to improve surveillance immediately and must consider the report since in the very near future we will have to provide a massive capability, requiring a massive infusion of funds, to protect not only our fishing resources but our oil and mineral resources, as well as to build up the economy of Canada and-

Mr. Speaker, at the outset I want to say that I think the hon. member is quite right to question the capability of Canada to patrol and survey, as well as provide search and rescue facilities in, an expanded zone off our coasts. However, when he put his question in the House on April 8 the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) made it clear at that time that the various departments involved are preparing plans to carry out that task. He also made it clear that, as the need arose, additional equipment would be acquired to carry out the tasks referred to by the hon. member.
In his question the hon. member referred to foreign fishing fleets operating in our economic zone if and when we declare a 200 mile limit, and I share his view that we will definitely declare such a zone. I agree this is a legitimate concern. However, it is worthy of note, I think, that perhaps the best way to preserve our fishing stocks, particularly in that expanded zone, is through negotiated agreements and then being able, following agreement, to put them in force. Canada has already negotiated agreements with the four major fishing nations off our coasts. I think it is also worth nothing that some figures I saw the other day, which I believe the hon. member also saw, indicated that it was not foreign fishing fleets off our shores but Canadian vessels which were the biggest offenders in regard to the ICNAF quotas.
I should also point out that at the present time the boundaries of Canada's search and rescue responsibility are much larger than the 200 mile zone, and they are recognized both by the International Civil Aviation Organization and the International Maritime Consultative Organization. The military air search facilities for which my minister is responsible are located at Summerside, P.E.I., right at the hub of the active search area, and as I say they cover a far greater area than 200 miles.
While the 200 mile economic zone has not yet been established, the Department of National Defence is making plans to cover this is limit adequately once it is established. Planning is being conducted with the Department

subtopic: TRANSPORT-POSSIBLE ABANDONMENT OF RAIL SERVICE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID CRISIS
TRANSPORT-POSSIBLE ABANDONMENT OF RAIL SERVICE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I am raising tonight is a follow-up to the question I put to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) on March 26 having to do with the possibility of rail line abandonment in Prince Edward Island. The importance of this subject has been stressed as recently as last Saturday, in an article in the Globe and Mail on Prince Edward Island's rail situation, entitled "Railways in Danger."
At the time I put my question on March 26 I asked the Minister of Transport mainly to comment on the statements made on more than one occasion by the provincial minister of highways with regard to the very serious situation concerning the railroad in Prince Edward Island, and the report which came from one of the minister's colleagues, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) before the Standing Committee on Regional Development, a report which said that the situation in respect of transportation in Prince Edward Island was in fact reaching a crisis stage and should be dealt with very shortly if we were not to be faced with a situation which would literally be irreversible. The reason I raise this matter again this evening is that apparently there have been meetings between the Minister of Transport and the provincial minister of highways, Mr. Stewart.
Perhaps it would be useful to give the nature of the problem in brief form through quotations which have appeared in articles over the last month and a half. I shall quote first from the Globe and Mail of last Saturday which is perhaps the best article at this stage in respect of the situation as it pertains to Prince Edward Island. It states;
Prince Edward Island, the first province to have all its steam locomotives replaced by diesels and the first to lose passenger service, may soon be the first to do without the railway entirely.
At a glance, the rail system looks adequate. True, 22 of 27 railway stations have been closed but derelict stations are national landmarks. And, although Canadian National hopes to gain permission from the Canadian Transport Commission to scrap a couple of branch lines this

May 3, 1976
Adjournment Debate
year, there are still more than 200 miles of track, down only 20 or 30 miles from the railway's peak.
However,-
This is really the important part of the question before us this evening.
-the railbeds have been allowed to deteriorate to the point where all trains are forced to move at a crawl and the ancient and inadequate cars relegated to hauling island produce are being scrapped at the rate of more than 100 a year.
The situation has been reported in the provincial legislature at its sessions this year. Again I am quoting from an article in the Summerside Journal. It refers to a statement by Mr. Stewart:
'The handwriting is on the wall,' he said, 'road bed maintenance has deteriorated with all trains running on' "slow order". He said in some cases there are areas where train traffic is slowed down to 10 miles per hour on road beds.
Unfortunately this is not a new but rather a continuing situation which indicates again the lack of study and the totally dreadful approach taken by the CNR in respect of its obligation to Prince Edward Island. I say it is doubly disturbing not only because this Crown corporation is committed to providing some form of national railway service, and it has certainly shown a great default in this instance, but in addition there is the fact that one of the major commitments the federal government made at the time of Confederation in 1873 was not only to maintain a continuous ferry service from Prince Edward Island to the mainland but also to provide a train service to transport basic Island produce.
This is the situation which confronts the government today. I think it should take swift and definite action in respect of the CNR. It is perhaps a little ironic that we are discussing this matter at a time when the CNR has already announced increases up to 69 per cent on the car ferry service operating between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. This is a case in which the CNR has definitely defaulted on its obligation.
One of the reasons why I put this question down for the adjournment debate-and I do not like to say this-is the rather cavalier attitude of the Minister of Transport. His answer to me on March 26 was:
Mr. Speaker, we always attempt to analyse trends in traffic and to look ahead to the steps that have to be taken to accommodate them, and this is what we are doing in this case.
That, Mr. Speaker, is no assurance at all. It is a denial of the federal government's obligation and responsibility.
It is a well known fact that there is no way possible- and the minister of highways reaffirmed this in the legislature recently-in which we can make an orderly transfer from the utilization of the railroad traffic both to move our basic produce out of the province or to bring in items to P.E.I., except perhaps over a five to ten year period. Both the time period required to upgrade the highways and to handle the amount of increased traffic that would occur through lack of railroads as well as additional cost, which would certainly be in the order of $20 million or more, would make it an almost prohibitive option at this time. Therefore I trust that my good friend, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), parliamentary secretary to the minister, will be able to assure me and the people of P.E.I. tonight that in fact the government is taking definite

action to make sure that CNR does not achieve by its neglect the total abandonment of railroad service in P.E.I.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-POSSIBLE ABANDONMENT OF RAIL SERVICE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND-GOVERNMENT ACTION TO AVOID CRISIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to begin with I must say I regret the reference which the hon. member has made to some sort of cavalier attitude on the part of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) in this situation, or in any situation with regard to transportation matters in Canada. His attitude is surely not that, as I think has been amply demonstrated in the House and in public forums outside the House, and certainly at his meetings with his provincial counterparts from the Atlantic region and other regions. I regret indeed any inference to the effect that his attitude can be interpreted in any way as being cavalier. It is a very serious one, and he does wish very much indeed to develop in this country from coast to coast the very best kind of transportation system that we can possibly develop.
My hon. friend on March 26 first raised this issue concerning the possible abandonment of rail service by CNR in Prince Edward Island. I would like to assure the House that no application has been made by CNR to the Canadian Transport Commission for such an abandonment.
May I also assure the House, and my hon. friend as well, that both the Railway Act and the National Transportation Act seek to protect shippers for the sake of the public interest with respect to the provision of essential services. That is to say that within the normal process that is established by statute, railway services are not allowed to be abandoned unilaterally by the railways. The railways must first make an application to the CTC and then, as hon. members know, the CTC holds public hearings in the national interest, and one of the key matters which is always considered is whether or not an alternative transportation facility or service is available to the area being served. Only after such hearings, and after due consideration has been given to the provision of alternative means would the CTC make a decision on an application.
At this point there is only one CN application in front of the CTC for the abandonment of nine miles of spur track. A hearing on this 1972 application has tentatively been scheduled by the CTC for later this year, but this will depend on priorities, such as passenger hearings for example.
There does not appear to be imminent danger that the existing rail system would not be adequate to meet immediate requirements. As to longer term needs, Transport Canada is working in conjunction with other federal departments, the railways, the provincial governments, and the local market boards to determine the nature and shape of an efficient and economic transportation system which could be implemented to deliver products to the major market areas.
